hints: Focus on what the word oxidation really means here, gaining oxygen or losing electrons to form a cleaner product.
Check which two pollutants are in a reduced, fuel-like form and can still pick up more oxygen, $\text{CO}$ and unburnt hydrocarbons.
Think about what must happen to $\text{NO}_2$ instead, it needs to lose oxygen to become $\text{N}_2$, so that is reduction not oxidation.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a catalytic converter does**

A modern converter does two jobs at once. It oxidises some pollutants and reduces others, all on a platinum, palladium and rhodium surface.

Remember: oxidation = gain of oxygen, reduction = loss of oxygen.

**Oxidise carbon monoxide**

$\text{CO}$ is formed by incomplete combustion. It can still gain oxygen to become the much less toxic $\text{CO}_2$.

$$2\text{CO} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2$$

**Oxidise unburnt hydrocarbons**

Unburnt hydrocarbons, e.g. $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}$, are also fuel fragments. They are oxidised completely to carbon dioxide and water.

$$\text{hydrocarbon} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Reduce nitrogen dioxide**

$\text{NO}_2$ is already highly oxidised. It cannot be oxidised further, it is reduced to harmless nitrogen by losing oxygen.

$$2\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{N}_2 + 2\text{O}_2$$

So only 1 and 3 are removed by oxidation.

options.A: Incorrect. While 1 and 3 are oxidised, 2 is not. Nitrogen dioxide is removed by reduction to N2, not by oxidation, so including all three is wrong.
options.B: Incorrect. Unburnt hydrocarbons (1) are indeed oxidised, but nitrogen dioxide (2) is reduced, not oxidised. This choice also wrongly leaves out carbon monoxide which is oxidised.
options.C: Correct. Both unburnt hydrocarbons (1) and carbon monoxide (3) are oxidised in the converter to CO2 and H2O. Nitrogen dioxide (2) is removed separately by reduction.
options.D: Incorrect. Carbon monoxide (3) is correctly oxidised, but nitrogen dioxide (2) is reduced to nitrogen, not oxidised. This choice also wrongly leaves out unburnt hydrocarbons.
